summary: A white paper with personal opinions on IPng engineering considerations, drawing on experience with the DECnet Phase V transition. It suggests splitting IPng decisions and transition tasks into smaller parts. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Advice to break one huge job into smaller jobs, so experts can work on each one early.

subtitle: Breaking IPng decisions into manageable parts, informed by DECnet transition experience.

tldr.problem: A single monolithic IPng decision is too complex and delays solutions to individual problems.
tldr.mechanism: Break the IPng challenge into smaller, independent parts (addressing, name service, host software, routing) so experts can tackle them in parallel with appropriate urgency.
tldr.outcome: Faster progress because non-blocking decisions (like routing changes) can proceed while slower ones (like administrative changes) get the lead time they need.

today: RFC 1670 is an Informational RFC from 1994. It documents thinking in the IPng design discussions that led to IPv6. The principles it advocates—modular decisions and local autonomy in transition—influenced how IPv6 was eventually planned and deployed.

sections.title: Breaking Down the Challenge
sections.content:
RFC 1670 is a white paper from Denise Heagerty at CERN, written in response to the IPng solicitation. Heagerty draws on experience managing the transition from DECnet Phase IV to Phase V across a large physics research network. The core argument is simple: treat IPng not as one massive decision, but as a collection of related but separable choices.

The RFC identifies four key areas that need decisions: address structure and allocation, name service changes, host software and programming interfaces, and routing protocol changes. While all are interconnected, they do not need the same deadline.
sections.eli5: Heagerty says instead of making one big decision about the Internet, split it into four smaller decisions: addresses, naming, software on computers, and routing.

sections.title: Timescales and Dependencies
sections.content:
The RFC argues that administrative decisions, especially those affecting address assignment, need the most time. Organizations must plan, budgeted changes, deploy new systems, and retire old ones. Ten years or more of lead time is realistic. Routing protocol changes, by contrast, can happen quickly because routers update without affecting the hosts they serve.

The RFC recommends early commitment on address structure and enough detail for service managers to start planning. Hosts that cannot be upgraded should be phased out or configured with reduced connectivity, a plan that takes years.
sections.eli5: Changing how addresses work takes the longest because so many physical things have to change. Routing is faster because it just means updating routers.

sections.title: Transition and Local Control
sections.content:
The RFC stresses that transition must respect local autonomy. Service managers close to their users understand the constraints (financial, political and technical) in their own environments. Provide them with a transition toolbox, scenarios and examples so they can adapt solutions locally.

Systems and sites should be able to transition at different times. A feedback loop based on real-world experience will improve software. Identify what software must change and keep the list current.
sections.eli5: Let each organization change to the new Internet on their own schedule, with tools and examples to help them decide what to do.

sections.title: Administration and Configuration
sections.content:
CERN runs IP on diverse equipment and operating systems. The RFC notes needs for efficient configuration: a way to send each system its IP parameters (address, default router, name servers) and to collect data from systems (contact, location, name). Automatic configuration would ease the tight coupling of addresses to physical subnets.

As the network grows, hierarchical address and routing delegation becomes critical. Breaking addresses into multiple hierarchy levels lets management devolve into subdomains.
sections.eli5: Networks need easy ways to tell a computer its address and find out where it is, and a way to split management into smaller regions.

references.text: Gross, P. (ed.), "Internet Next Generation Architecture", RFC 1550, December 1993.
